storm.summary_layperson: Scattered thunderstorm chances build in tonight from the west, and the Sound's cooling effect isn't quite strong enough this evening to guarantee its usual protection, so the cove could see these storms close to full strength.
storm.local_effect_blurb: Air-water gap is 8.3°F, just under the ~10°F needed for the protective marine layer to kick in, and with shear aloft topping 35-40 kt, the sea-breeze convergence could let storms intensify at the coast rather than choke as they usually do here.
storm.detail_html:
Radar (KOKX) shows a cluster of cells near 40 dBZ, about 33 miles west of the cove, drifting ESE at roughly 14 kt. CAPE is low right now (100 J/kg) but the HRRR run has it building sharply overnight to 1,200-1,700 J/kg by late evening, alongside strong 0-6km bulk shear holding in the 30-40 kt range through the window. The OKX forecast discussion flags "increasing chances of showers and thunderstorms tonight into early Thursday," with some storms potentially producing strong wind gusts, and notes ample shear even though capping may limit how much CAPE actually develops.

Normally the cool Long Island Sound (74.1°F water vs 82.4°F air) would set up a protective marine layer that chokes low-level convection before it reaches the cove — that's the mechanism that often leaves Riverside with wind but not much rain while inland spots get hit harder. Tonight the gap is 8.3°F, which is meaningful but sits just under the ~10°F threshold the pipeline uses to call the mechanism active, so it is not currently flagged as protective despite the Sound-effect "likelihood" reading high on approach geometry and storm speed alone.

That absence matters more because the sea breeze is active this afternoon and shear is running well above the 35 kt threshold where things flip from protective to counterproductive: strong, organized storms can punch through or even intensify at the coastal convergence boundary instead of dying there. Combined with no marine-layer buffer, that tips tonight's local effect from neutral toward amplifying rather than the more typical Riverside story of storms fizzling at the shoreline.

The lead cell is closing, radar-tracked at 33.5 miles out and closing near 13 kt, projecting an ETA around 6:23 PM (window 5:51-6:54 PM, medium confidence — radar-measured motion but still over an hour out). Neither the marine-layer nor sea-breeze discount applies to this cell's arrival, so treat the ETA as this cell's expected strength at arrival, not a weakened version of it.

A Coastal Flood Statement (minor) is in effect for the area overnight into early Thursday morning — that's a tidal/coastal flooding advisory, unrelated to the thunderstorm threat, and doesn't change the storm call.

Bottom line: keep an eye on radar through the evening. This isn't a case where Victor can assume the Sound will blunt the first wave — bring things in and watch for the 6-7 PM window, then reassess as additional cells develop overnight with rising CAPE.

arrival.blurb: Radar-tracked cell 33 mi W closing at about 13 kt, arriving with no marine-layer buffer (8.3°F gap, just under the protective threshold) and into 35+ kt shear — expect it near full strength.

wind.regime_label: Sea-breeze day — thermal still filling in
wind.tactics_blurb: A pure thermal sea breeze is filling in from the south, but the signal is still weak and patchy across the wider coast — expect it to firm up over the next hour, hold through about 7:00-7:15 PM, then fade fast into sunset (7:56 PM). Favor the center of the course and don't expect much past the second race.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
This is a sea-breeze day, but a weak and immature one. The two-ingredient test is met on paper — the air-water temperature gap (deltaT) is 8.3°F, well above the 5°F threshold — but the sea breeze itself is only lightly established: just 16% of coastal stations are confirming southerly flow, well short of what a fully mature thermal usually shows by mid-afternoon. RYC (ground truth for the cove) is already reading S at 177°, 2.6 kt, gusting 5.4, 10-min average 3.8 kt — a real but light and puffy signal.

The gradient wind near the cove itself is light and offshore-ish (inland/west-zone stations cluster W-NW around 3-6 kt), which is why this reads as pure thermal (Regime A) rather than a gradient-reinforced sea breeze (A+) — the background flow isn't adding to the thermal here, though stations further east on the Sound (Groton, Westerly) are showing more SW flow at 9-10 kt. That split is a reminder this is a local, still-consolidating sea-breeze cell, not a Sound-wide established flow yet.

Worth flagging: RYC's current S 177° reading diverges sharply (~100°) from the broader west-zone ensemble median (W 278°), which is itself unreliable right now — most of the calm APRS stations feeding that average are reading under 1 kt, where direction is essentially noise. Trust RYC for the cove-specific call; the model (HRRR) briefly showed a stray WNW read at 5 PM before snapping back to south by 6 PM, which we're treating as model lag/noise rather than a real shift.

Expect the breeze to keep building and veering slightly through 6-7 PM, then fade quickly — the pipeline projects the sea breeze collapsing around 7:26 PM, about 30 minutes ahead of sunset (7:56 PM). After that, don't expect much: light and variable for an hour or so, then a gradient-driven southerly fills back in later in the evening (7, then 7 kt by 9-10 PM) as the overnight storm system approaches — that's synoptic flow ahead of the thunderstorm chances, not a sea breeze.

With S/SSW the dominant direction through the window, pressure should stay fairly uniform across the cove — favor the center of the course rather than either shore. Given the weak, still-ramping signal, treat early shifts as persistent (righting) rather than tactical oscillations; only play shifts actively once it's clearly mature, likely not before 6 PM.

data_caveats: Buoy 44040 (WLIS Sound sensor) observation is about 106 min old — treat offshore SST/wind as slightly stale.

Sea-breeze direction signal is weak and inconsistent: RYC reads S at the cove while the broader coastal ensemble median points W, and only 16% of coastal stations confirm southerly flow — an early, still-localized sea breeze rather than a regionally established one.
